22539-rock-a-bye-library-a-book-of-fable:
Rock-a-Bye Library is a book of fables for good little children. Aesop's old tales fill its pages in simple, clear retellings. One fable opens with a cock scratching straw in a farmyard.

Scratching for food for the hens, the cock finds a jewel. Ho, said he, you are a very fine thing, no doubt. Those who prize you may value you highly, he concedes. But give me a barley-corn before all the world's pearls. The moral lands plainly for young readers to grasp easily. Fables like this taught sense through animal actors for centuries. The volume's promise is amusement joined to instruction. Its short tales suit reading aloud at bedtime.
33986-comic-tragedies-written-by-jo-and-:
Louisa May Alcott, as Jo, and her sister Anna, as Meg, wrote these comic tragedies in girlhood, acted by the Little Women and published in Boston in 1893. A foreword by Meg recalls the big garret where, after teaching, sewing, and helping mother, the girls turned themselves into queens and knights for dramatic revels.

The plays run from Norna, or The Witch's Curse, and The Captive of Castile to The Greek Slave, Ion, Bianca, and The Unloved Wife. The volume, copyrighted by Anna B. Pratt, preserves the Alcott sisters' youthful stage work. It charms readers who love Little Women and its world.
4596-unknown-to-history-a-story-of-the-c:
Charlotte M. Yonge published Unknown to History in 1882, as a story of the captivity of Mary, Queen of Scots. Her preface names her sources in Strickland's life of Mary and Burton's history of Scotland, and she admits that she cut some incidents and persons to keep the tale clear. She aimed less at a minute sifting of facts than at a view of noted characters in remarkable situations, and at the report on which her tale rests.

The contents open with a little waif, evil tidings, and the captive herself, then move through an oak hall, a huckstering woman, a bewitched whistle, and the key of a cipher. Babington's plot shadows the later chapters, as loyalty and treason pull at Mary's household. Readers get a careful historical romance for young and old, where a hidden child and a captive queen share one dangerous, closely watched world.
britannica-1911-axolotl:
Axolotl is the Mexican name for larval salamanders of the genus Amblystoma, creatures long eaten in Mexico and sold in its markets. Cuvier first saw that these gilled water animals were not kin to Siren and Proteus, as most placed them, but the young form of an air-breathing salamander.

Proof took half a century. Axolotls were found breeding while still wearing their gills, which seemed to settle the case against Cuvier under the genus name Siredon. Later finds showed Siredon is only the larva of Amblystoma, a salamander long known across North America, and Cuvier was right. The entry then describes the larva itself: plump body, crested tail, large head, and limbs, growing to eleven inches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Zwettl, a filiation of Heiligenkreuz in the Morimond line, stands in Lower Austria in the Diocese of Saint Hippolyte. Hadmar the First of Kuenring founded it in 1137, with Herrmann of Heiligenkreuz as first abbot. Innocent the Second confirmed the foundation in 1140, and other popes and emperors followed. Church, chapter-room, and dormitory received blessing in 1159, though the whole monastery was finished only in 1218.

For over two centuries Zwettl flourished in spirit and wealth, then declined and was repeatedly plundered, sacked and burned in 1426 with one brother martyred. Abbot John rebuilt it from 1437, and it regained splendour until the Reformation cut it to six monks and one secular priest and sold a fourth of its lands. Later abbots revived it: Erasmus, Linck the annalist, and Melchior, who rebuilt much of the abbey and founded its library. After a commendatory abbot under Josephinism, the monks again elected their abbot from 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernando-de-a:
Fernando de Alba Ixtlilxochitl was a native Mexican historian of royal descent. Born in 1568, he descended from Netzahualpilli, king of Texcoco. Educated at Santa Cruz de Tlaltelolco, he lived long in dire poverty. His works pleaded for his family's land, relief, and rights.

His Historia de la Nacion Chichimeca, left unfinished at the siege of Mexico, is his best work. It draws on paintings, traditions, and songs, all more than eighty years old. His chronology there is exact, his editing careful and clear. He died in 1648, the most illustrious of native Mexican historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-hyrtl:
Joseph Hyrtl was an Austrian anatomist ranked among the great teachers of the nineteenth century. Born at Eisenstadt in Hungary in 1810 to poor parents, he began medicine at Vienna in 1831 and paid his way by making anatomical preparations. At twenty-six he took the anatomy chair at Prague, where he finished his famous textbook of human anatomy.

Called to Vienna in 1845, he published the first textbook of applied, or topographic, anatomy in 1850. His courses drew crowds of students and doctors, and his fame spread across Europe. In 1865, at the university's five-hundredth anniversary, he was chosen rector as its most distinguished member.
unknown-to-history-a-story-of-the-captiv:
Charlotte M. Yonge built her novel Unknown to History on the captivity of Mary Queen of Scots. In a preface dated February 27, 1882, she points readers to the report behind her tale, found in Miss Strickland's Life of Mary Queen of Scots and in Burton's History of Scotland. She warns that she has cut some facts about the captivity and the Babington plot, and left out many real people of the queen's household, to keep the story clear.

The contents open with a little waif, evil tidings, and the captive, then move to a bewitched whistle, the key of a cipher, and unquiet days. A companion record of the same book carries the same preface, with a contents list that runs further. Yonge aimed at readers who want noted people in striking scenes more than a full sifting of proof, and her preface says so in plain terms.
